units.title: Unit 37 — Making a career
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 37. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Job searching, career progression and employment
learningObjectives: Describe applying for jobs, writing applications and CVs, and attending interviews.
Use employ, employment, unemployed and related word families in accurate work contexts.
Talk about workplace training, experience, promotion and pay rises.
Distinguish choosing to resign or quit from being sacked by an employer.
Describe part-time and full-time work, professional success, ownership and retirement.

items.pt: candidatar-se a uma vaga de emprego
items.example: She decided to apply for a job at the local hospital.
items.note: Apply for a job or position means request to be considered for it.

items.example: You can apply online before Friday.
items.note: In a career context, apply is usually followed by for when naming the position.

items.example: Her application reached the company yesterday.
items.note: Noun related to apply; often used in job application.

items.pt: carta de candidatura; carta de apresentação para uma vaga
items.example: He wrote a letter of application for the teaching post.
items.note: A letter explaining why you want a position and why you are suitable.

items.example: Please email your CV before the interview.
items.note: British English abbreviation of curriculum vitae; describes education and work experience.

items.example: She sent out ten CVs during her job search.
items.note: Send out means distribute documents to several recipients.

items.example: He felt confident during his first job interview.
items.note: An interview is a meeting where an employer checks whether an applicant is suitable.

items.pt: fazer uma entrevista; participar de uma entrevista
items.example: I've got to have an interview on Tuesday morning.
items.note: Common collocation for attending a recruitment interview.

items.example: The firm employs twenty people.
items.note: An employer employs someone, giving them paid work.

items.example: More people are employed in the town this year.
items.note: Employed means having paid work; opposite: unemployed.

items.example: The new factory created opportunities for employment.
items.note: Uncountable in this general sense; related to employ and employed.

items.example: The company gave new staff training during their first week.
items.note: Training is uncountable in this context: say some training, not a training.

items.example: All new workers receive training before using the machines.
items.note: Training is generally uncountable; contrast a training course.

items.example: She completed a training course in customer service.
items.note: A countable course that provides organised instruction in a skill.

items.pt: participar de um curso de capacitação
items.example: I'm going to go on a training course next month.
items.note: British English uses go on a course to mean attend it.

items.pt: promover no trabalho; elevar de cargo
items.example: The company plans to promote her to team leader.
items.note: To give someone a higher-level role, often with more responsibility.

items.example: He was promoted after two years in the department.
items.note: Passive construction for receiving a promotion.

items.example: Her promotion brought new responsibilities.
items.note: A move to a more senior position; noun related to promote.

items.example: The workers asked for a pay rise after a busy year.
items.note: British English expression meaning an increase in pay.

items.pt: dar um aumento de salário a alguém
items.example: The manager gave the team a pay rise in January.
items.note: Use give someone a pay rise, not give someone a rise of pay.

items.example: Working in a small company gave her valuable experience.
items.note: Uncountable for general knowledge and skill gained by doing a job.

items.example: A promotion usually means more responsibility.
items.note: A duty or a set of things that someone must take care of.

items.example: My boss encouraged me to apply for the role.
items.note: An informal or neutral term for the person who manages your work.

items.pt: pedir demissão; deixar o cargo voluntariamente
items.example: She decided to resign after accepting another job.
items.note: Resign means choose to leave your position; unlike be sacked.

items.pt: pedido de demissão; renúncia ao cargo
items.example: The director announced his resignation on Friday.
items.note: The act or announcement of voluntarily leaving a job or position.

items.example: I won't quit my job until I find a better one.
items.note: Quit is less formal than resign; both can describe voluntary departure.

items.pt: trabalhar no exterior; trabalhar em outro país
items.example: She wants to work abroad for a few years.
items.note: Abroad means in or to another country.

items.example: After moving to Leeds, he began to look for a job.
items.note: Look for describes searching; apply for describes seeking a specific position.

items.example: He got a job in a hotel near the station.
items.note: Get a job means secure paid employment.

items.pt: ficar farto de algo; cansar-se de uma situação
items.example: After months of delays, he got fed up with the project.
items.note: Informal: become tired or annoyed by something continuing.

items.example: The company sacked him for repeatedly arriving late.
items.note: British English and informal: dismiss an employee; contrasts with resign.

items.example: The owner gave the dishonest employee the sack.
items.note: Informal British expression for dismissing an employee.

items.example: He was unemployed for three months after the factory closed.
items.note: Opposite of employed; describes a person without a job.

items.example: Unemployment fell after the new businesses opened.
items.note: The state or level of people being without paid work.

items.example: Several people were out of work after the hotel closed.
items.note: Common phrase meaning unemployed, not simply away from the office.

items.pt: emprego de meio período; trabalho em jornada parcial
items.example: She has a part-time job while studying.
items.note: A job involving fewer working hours than a full-time position.

items.pt: emprego de tempo integral; trabalho em jornada integral
items.example: He's looking for a full-time job after university.
items.note: Opposite of a part-time job.

items.pt: trabalhar em tempo parcial; trabalhar meio período
items.example: I work part-time so I can study in the evenings.
items.note: Part-time describes the working schedule, not a separate kind of occupation.

items.example: She works full-time at a local engineering firm.
items.note: Full-time is used adverbially after work.

items.example: He hasn't had a job since April.
items.note: Job is countable; use have a job rather than have a work.

items.example: Her small business became successful within two years.
items.note: Adjective related to success and succeed.

items.example: The restaurant's success surprised its owner.
items.note: Can describe an achievement or a general positive outcome.

items.pt: ter sucesso; conseguir atingir um objetivo
items.example: You can succeed without working in a large company.
items.note: Verb; often succeed in something or succeed in doing something.

items.example: Her parents own two small restaurants.
items.note: Verb referring to possession; own as an adjective means belonging to oneself.

items.example: I'd like to start my own business one day.
items.note: Own emphasises personal ownership, not employment by another company.

items.example: The owner of the café greeted every customer.
items.note: Person who owns something; formed from own.

items.example: My aunt plans to retire next summer.
items.note: Stop working permanently, usually because of age.

items.example: His retired neighbour volunteers at the library.
items.note: Adjective describing someone who has stopped regular paid work.

items.example: He hopes to travel more after retirement.
items.note: Noun corresponding to retire.

items.example: She wants to build a career in software engineering.
items.note: Long-term progress through a profession or working life.

B · Promotion: responsibility, pay rise, experience and promotion
C · Resignation: work abroad, quit, resign and finding a job
D · Unemployment: fed up, sack, out of work, part-time and full-time, including common-mistake box

units.title: Unit 38 — Working in an office
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 38. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Office equipment, administration and workplace problems
learningObjectives: Identify common British-English office equipment and distinguish diary, calendar, filing cabinet and files.
Use everyday office verbs and collocations for correspondence, invoices, appointments and visitors.
Connect arrange, attend, organise and produce with their related nouns.
Describe routine office work and use involve followed by a noun or an -ing form.
Report equipment failures, missing supplies, absent colleagues and a heavy workload.

items.example: Our office is on the second floor.
items.note: A place where administrative or professional work is done.

items.example: The meeting schedule is on the noticeboard.
items.note: British English term for a board displaying announcements.

items.example: We keep a wall calendar beside the door.
items.note: Shows dates, months and often scheduled events; unlike a diary, it is not necessarily a personal appointment book.

items.example: The photocopier is beside the printer.
items.note: A machine that makes paper copies of documents.

items.pt: armário de arquivos; gaveteiro para documentos
items.example: Old contracts are stored in the filing cabinet.
items.note: A cabinet, often with drawers, for organising papers.

items.example: I wrote the appointment in my diary.
items.note: In British English, diary may mean a book for appointments and plans.

items.example: She used a calculator to check the total.
items.note: An electronic or other device for doing calculations.

items.example: My new keyboard is much quieter than the old one.
items.note: A set of keys used to type into a computer.

items.example: Put the unwanted papers in the rubbish bin.
items.note: British English; bin is the container, and rubbish is waste.

items.example: Keep the customer files in this cupboard.
items.note: Here files refers to collections of documents, often in folders.

items.example: The printer is running out of paper.
items.note: Useful contextual equipment named in the office-problems section.

items.example: The company produces furniture for hotels.
items.note: Verb, stressed on the second syllable; related noun production.

items.example: Production increased when the company bought new machines.
items.note: Noun formed from the verb produce.

items.example: The factory makes furniture for small offices.
items.note: Normally uncountable: some furniture, not furnitures.

items.example: The factory is across the road from the main office.
items.note: A building where goods are manufactured.

items.pt: envolver; incluir como parte do trabalho
items.example: My job involves checking technical reports.
items.note: Follow involve with a noun or an -ing form, not to + infinitive.

items.example: I finished the paperwork before going home.
items.note: Uncountable; paperwork includes forms, reports and other documents.

items.example: She had to type a letter to the supplier.
items.note: Type means write text using a computer keyboard.

items.example: He can type without looking at the keyboard.
items.note: Verb for producing text using keys; noun type has other senses.

items.pt: enviar faturas ou notas de cobrança
items.example: We send out invoices at the end of each month.
items.note: Send out means distribute or send documents to recipients.

items.example: The supplier emailed an invoice for the new chairs.
items.note: Document stating goods or services supplied and how much is owed.

items.example: The customer asked for a copy of the invoice.
items.note: Someone who purchases goods or services.

items.example: I send emails to suppliers every morning.
items.note: Common routine communication activity described in the source.

items.example: Can you arrange a visit for our new clients?
items.note: Arrange means plan or prepare for something to happen.

items.example: We made arrangements for the visitors' transport.
items.note: Noun related to arrange; often plural for practical plans.

items.pt: organizar uma visita; agendar uma visita
items.example: She arranged a visit to the company's new factory.
items.note: The verb arrange emphasises planning ahead.

items.pt: marcar um horário; agendar um compromisso
items.example: I'd like to make an appointment with the bank manager.
items.note: Use make an appointment when scheduling a meeting or service.

items.example: My appointment is at half past two.
items.note: A planned time to see someone for a professional purpose.

items.example: She organises the office party every December.
items.note: British spelling: organise; manage and plan an event or activity.

items.example: Good organisation makes events easier to manage.
items.note: Noun related to organise; can also mean an institution.

items.pt: mostrar as instalações aos visitantes; conduzir uma visita
items.example: The receptionist showed the visitors round the office.
items.note: British English; show someone round means give them a tour of a place.

items.example: I need to attend a meeting this afternoon.
items.note: Attend takes a direct object: attend a meeting, not attend to a meeting in this sense.

items.example: Attendance at the workshop was higher than expected.
items.note: Noun connected with attend.

items.pt: participar de uma reunião; comparecer à reunião
items.example: She attends a team meeting every Wednesday.
items.note: Attend means be present at the meeting; arrange means set it up.

items.example: The meeting begins at ten.
items.note: An organised event where people discuss matters.

items.example: Ordering supplies is one of my weekly tasks.
items.note: A particular piece of work that needs to be done.

items.pt: organização de viagens; providências de viagem
items.example: The assistant handles travel arrangements for the team.
items.note: Plans such as transport and accommodation, used in an exercise.

items.example: A colleague helped me finish the report.
items.note: Someone who works with you, often in the same organisation.

items.example: The photocopier broke down just before the meeting.
items.note: Intransitive phrasal verb meaning stop working; said of machinery and vehicles.

items.example: The office computer isn't working today.
items.note: A natural alternative to say that a device is faulty or broken.

items.pt: ficar sem algo; esgotar o estoque de algo
items.example: We ran out of printer paper this morning.
items.note: Run out of means have none left; something names the missing supply.

items.example: The office ran out of paper during the morning.
items.note: Frequently used with office supplies such as paper and ink.

items.example: We ran out of ink before printing the forms.
items.note: Exercise context: a printer cannot print when there is no ink left.

items.example: Two team members were absent because of illness.
items.note: Describes someone who is not present where expected.

items.pt: estar ausente do trabalho; estar de folga
items.example: The manager is off today, so call her tomorrow.
items.note: Off can mean away from work rather than not working properly.

items.pt: muito; muitos; uma grande quantidade de
items.example: We've got loads of emails to answer.
items.note: Informal expression meaning a lot of.

items.example: We've got loads of work before the holiday.
items.note: Work is uncountable in this sense; loads of is informal.

items.example: We're busy preparing for the conference.
items.note: Being busy describes having many things to do.
